title: Children in overcrowded homes get poorer GCSE results, study finds
summary:
Researchers urge ministers to ensure young people in rented homes have space for a desk in their bedroom

Children who share a bedroom and lack a quiet place to study at home get worse GCSE…

blocks.text: Children who share a bedroom and lack a quiet place to study at home get worse GCSE results than their peers, according to a major report on how poor housing affects education.

The research, carried out by leading academics at University College London for the Sutton Trust, a social mobility charity, urged UK ministers to ensure all young people in rented accommodation have space for a desk.

Nick Harrison, the chief executive of the trust, said: “The country’s housing crisis is blighting the prospects of a generation. The link between a child’s housing situation and their education shouldn’t be underestimated.
“Even the brightest child will struggle to succeed at school if they don’t have a safe and stable learning environment at home.”
The study found that children living in the worst housing conditions were less likely than their peers to get five good GCSEs, and less likely to get any A-levels.
The report called for a new policy ensuring children have a bedroom with space for a desk under the decent homes standard, a UK government benchmark for quality and safety in rented homes.

It also suggested schools and local authorities could be required to provide young people with access to quiet study space outside of the home, through extended opening hours, homework clubs and local libraries.

The record number of children living in temporary accommodation in England, which now stands at more than 170,000, is expected to exacerbate the attainment gap. The report found that those who had been homeless by age 14 were 18 percentage points less likely to achieve five good GCSEs.
The report’s co-author Gill Wyness, a professor of economics at UCL, said: “The raw differences between this homelessness experience, and GCSE and A level outcomes, were phenomenal.

“There are a bunch of kids out there who have to sit the same exams and are held to the same standard in their education, but don’t have the same conditions to learn in. It feels very unfair, and there are things we can do to improve this.”
Unlike previous research in this area, which normally considers a child’s access to learning materials and activities, academics looked at the “physical home learning environment” for children.
This was defined as whether they had their own bedroom, a quiet place to work and a home that was not considered overcrowded or noisy.

They found that young people from poorer families were more likely to lack space and a quiet place to study, and more than half (52%) of young people in the poorest fifth of families shared a bedroom at age 11, compared with 7% in the richest fifth.
The lack of a quiet place to study led to lower exam results: those who didn’t have a suitable study area scored lower at age 18 than their peers, despite being level at the end of primary school.
The report also found poor housing in childhood was linked to worse long-term employment, worse mental and physical health and lower life satisfaction into their mid-30s.

Each additional housing problem experienced by 11- to 15-year-old children left them three percentage points less likely to have a degree and three percentage points less likely to be in work in adulthood.
The Sutton Trust has called for a cross-departmental review of how housing policy impacts education, saying the Department for Education and the Ministry of Housing should work more closely.
Harrison said: “If we’re serious about improving educational outcomes and social mobility, we need to pay much greater attention to the housing circumstances in which young people are growing up.”
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Every child deserves the opportunity to build a better life and a safe, secure home is vital to this.”

She said the government was committed to ending the use of bed and breakfasts to house families and was putting a new duty on councils to ensure children in temporary accommodation get the support they need at school.
